user: I want to get a passport, what do I do?
assistant: To get a passport, you'll need to do the following: A separate appointment is required for processing each individual passport application.
Fill out an application form. Forms can be found online at https://eforms.state.gov. Provide proof of citizenship. This could be a previous passport, a certified birth certificate, a consular report of birth abroad, a naturalization certificate, or a certificate of citizenship. You must show identification such as a driver's license, a government ID, or a military ID.
Submit a passport photo. Recent Color Photograph: Photograph must meet passport requirements - full front view of the face, 2x2 inches in size, on a white background, and no eyeglasses. Pay the application fee.
Processing times can vary, so it's essential to apply well in advance of your planned travel dates. Please note, Processing times may have significant delays.
[The End of Previous Conversation]

[The Start of Current Turn Question]
Anything special I have to do for a 6 year old child?
[The End of Current Turn Question]

[The Start of Reference Answer]
Yes, there are some special requirements for a 6-year-old child. Both the child and both parents or legal guardians must appear and present the following:
* Form DS-11: Application for a U.S. Passport
* Proof of U.S. Citizenship, which can be an original birth certificate, Certificate of Citizenship, or Parent’s Naturalization Certificate + Child’s Permanent Resident Card
* Parental/Guardian Identification: Each parent must present original identification and submit a photocopy of the front and back with child’s application
* A recent color photograph that meets passport requirements. Full front view of the face, 2x2 inches in size, on a white background, and no eyeglasses.
 Also, if the child was born abroad, parent must provide evidence of the child’s U.S. Citizenship.
[The End of Reference Answer]

What can I do to protect children who are too young to get vaccinated?
Children younger than 6 months old are at high risk of serious flu complications, but are too young to get a flu vaccine. Because of this, safeguarding them from flu is especially important. If you live with or care for an infant younger than 6 months old, you should get a flu vaccine to help protect them from flu. Advice for Caregivers of Young Children is available for more information. Everyone else who is around the baby also should be vaccinated. Also, studies have shown that flu vaccination of the mother during pregnancy can protect the baby after birth from flu infection for several months.
In addition to getting vaccinated, you and your loved ones can take everyday preventive actions like staying away from sick people and washing your hands to reduce the spread of germs. If you are sick with flu, stay home from work or school to prevent spreading flu to others.

Keep a written description of the parent - their height, weight, hair and eye color, and a recent picture if you have one
Take full-faced pictures or videos of your child every 6 months
Enroll in the Children's Passport Issuance Alert program to get alerted about any passport applications for your child
The National Center for Missing and Exploited Children suggests that you teach your children to use the telephone, memorize your phone number and that you instruct them to call you immediately if anything unusual happens. 

Get legal advice. 
Talk to a lawyer about your concerns. They can advise you on your legal options to keep your child safe, such as getting a court order that restricts travel with your child or only allows supervised visitations.
